summary: This memo defines MIB objects for managing multiprotocol interconnect, including IP, traffic carried over X.25. It is historic.

eli5.summary: This paper lists the things a network manager can check about a connection that carries Internet traffic over an older telephone-company style network. It is historic.

questions: snmp objects for multiprotocol over x25
how to manage multiprotocol over x25
subtitle: Managing multiprotocol traffic over X.25 networks

tldr.problem: Network managers needed a way to monitor and control IP and other protocol traffic being sent over X.25 connections, including statistics about connection failures and address translation problems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1461 defines SNMP MIB objects organized into three tables: one for interface management, one for peer address information, and one for protocol encapsulation settings.
tldr.outcome: This specification became historic as X.25 networks were gradually replaced by IP-based technologies, but it was essential for managing the multiprotocol interconnect services of the 1990s.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Multiprotocol (IP, CLNP, ES-IS, SNAP) over X.25

today: RFC 1461 is Historic. X.25 was a common wide-area networking technology in the 1990s, but has been superseded by IP-based technologies. Modern networks no longer use multiprotocol interconnect over X.25.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1461 defines a set of management objects (called a MIB, or Management Information Base) that network administrators can use to monitor and control the transmission of multiprotocol traffic over X.25 networks. X.25 was an older packet-switched network technology commonly provided by telephone companies.

The objects allow a network manager to track the status of X.25 connections, count failures and statistics, configure timers, and manage the encapsulation of higher-layer protocols (IP, CLNP, ES-IS, and SNAP) within X.25 frames. These objects are accessed using SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol).
sections.eli5: This describes what a network manager can watch on a computer connection that sends Internet traffic over an older phone-company network.

sections.title: The Management Framework
sections.content:
The Network Management Framework consists of three parts: the SMI (Structure of Management Information), the MIB (the actual managed objects), and SNMP (the protocol for accessing them). RFC 1461 extends existing MIB definitions by adding objects specific to multiprotocol interconnect over X.25.

The objects defined in RFC 1461 work alongside other MIBs for X.25 itself (RFC 1382) and the lower layers (LAPB in RFC 1381). Together, they provide a complete picture of the X.25 protocol stack for management purposes.
sections.eli5: There is a standard way to organize things a computer network can report about itself. This RFC adds new things to report about one particular type of connection.

sections.title: The Three Tables
sections.content:
RFC 1461 defines three main tables of management objects. The mioxPleTable holds information about each X.25 interface (Packet Level Entity), including the maximum number of circuits allowed, counters for refused connections, and failures in translating between Internet addresses and X.121 addresses (the addressing scheme used by X.25).

The mioxPeerTable contains information about remote systems (peers) that can be contacted via X.25, including their X.121 addresses and call parameters. The mioxPeerEncTable extends the peer information with details about which protocol encapsulation type is used to communicate with each peer. All three tables are mandatory for conformance with the MIB.
sections.eli5: The MIB has three lists: one for each connection endpoint, one for known remote computers, and one for how to encode different protocol types when sending them.

sections.title: Statistics and Timers
sections.content:
Each interface in the mioxPleTable includes counters for tracking failures: the number of failed translations from Internet addresses to X.121 addresses, the number of failed translations in the opposite direction, and the number of Q-bit failures (a control signal failure in X.25). The RFC records the last failed address and the time of the most recent failure for each type of error.

The RFC also defines several configurable timers for managing connections: a minimum open timer (how long a connection must stay open), an inactivity timer (how long before an idle connection closes), a hold-down timer (how long to wait after a failed connection attempt), and a collision retry timer. These timers help the system manage X.25 resources efficiently.
sections.eli5: The manager can see when connections fail and why, and can set timers that control how long connections stay open or how long the system waits before trying again.

sections.title: Scope and Limitations
sections.content:
RFC 1461 applies only to X.25 interfaces that are actually carrying multiprotocol interconnect traffic. Nodes that implement RFC 1356 (which describes how to send IP over X.25) must implement this MIB. The objects apply to the software managing X.25 connections and protocol encapsulation, whether at a host, router, or bridge.

The RFC explicitly states that other software may also use X.25 (such as PAD, a Packet Assembler/Disassembler), but this MIB does not apply to such usage. The presence or operation of other X.25-based software will not affect these management objects.
sections.eli5: This MIB only describes the part that handles Internet traffic on X.25. Other software using X.25 for different purposes is not included.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content:
RFC 1461 is Historic. X.25 was a common wide-area networking technology in the 1990s, especially for international connections, but it has been superseded by IP-based technologies like Frame Relay and MPLS. Modern networks no longer use multiprotocol interconnect over X.25.

The RFC remains an important historical reference for understanding how network management worked for legacy systems and how the SNMP MIB framework was extended for specific technologies.
sections.eli5: This specification is historic because X.25 is no longer used on modern Internet networks.
